opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different things going on, and it's worth separating them out because people sometimes lump them together.

The first is just the compute economics. Pretraining scale-ups historically came in roughly 10x or more jumps in compute per generation, and each of those jumps takes a while to materialize. You need the datacenters, the chips, the power. So part of what looks like "slower progress from pretraining" is really that the next big scale-up just hasn't fully landed yet. The gap between generations has stretched out, and if you look in a window where there hasn't been a big new pretraining run, it can look like things are stalling when it's more that we're between steps.

The second thing is data. We've used a large fraction of the high-quality text that's readily available on the internet. You can keep going by repeating data, using lower-quality data, or generating synthetic data, but each of those has somewhat worse returns than fresh, high-quality human text. So the effective returns per unit of compute are probably getting a bit worse, though I don't think it's a hard wall.

Third, and I think this is underrated, the returns to pretraining loss improvements might be showing up in ways that are harder to see. Going from, say, a model that's quite smart to one that's somewhat smarter in a general, diffuse way doesn't necessarily produce an obvious jump on the benchmarks people are watching, especially when many of those benchmarks are already saturated or are dominated by what you get from post-training.

And relatedly, the fourth thing is that a lot of the action has shifted to RL and inference-time compute. Reinforcement learning on reasoning, agentic tasks, coding, that's been giving really large gains relatively cheaply. So labs rationally reallocate effort there, and pretraining looks comparatively less exciting. That doesn't mean pretraining has stopped working; it means the marginal dollar is getting more elsewhere right now.

So my overall take is: I'd update somewhat toward pretraining alone giving diminishing returns, maybe somewhat more than the naive scaling-law extrapolations people had a few years ago would suggest. But I'd be careful about overupdating. Overall AI progress doesn't look like it's slowing much, because RL scaling and other improvements are picking up the slack, and when the next big pretraining runs come in, we might see that the base models still get meaningfully better, which then makes the RL on top of them work better too. Those things compound.

r001.rationale: It says much of the high-quality text has been used and that lower-quality or repeated data gives worse returns, so returns per unit of compute are getting worse.

r002.rationale: It does not connect GPT-3 to GPT-4 improvements to using more high-quality training tokens as datasets grew.

r003.rationale: It says much of the readily available high-quality internet text has been used, but does not say that current data filtering captures the best available training data.

r004.rationale: It describes pretraining returns as diminishing while explicitly saying this is not a hard wall and that pretraining has not stopped working.

fable-5.1.text:
Ryan Greenblatt: Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on, and it's worth separating them out, because I think people sometimes conflate them.

The first thing is just that pretraining compute scaling has slowed down relative to the historical trend. For a while you had this situation where compute going into the biggest training runs was increasing something like 4x or 5x per year, and a decent chunk of that was going into pretraining specifically. But at some point the frontier labs started hitting practical constraints — how big a cluster you can actually build, power, how many chips you can get, how much you're willing to spend on a single run when you're not sure it'll pay off. So the raw scale-up of pretraining compute has been slower than people might have naively extrapolated from, say, 2020 to 2023.

The second thing is data. The classic Chinchilla-style scaling story says you want to scale data roughly in proportion to parameters, and the amount of high-quality human-written text is finite. People have been talking about the "data wall" for a while, and I think it's real, though it's more of a gradual headwind than a hard wall. You can do things like multi-epoch training, use synthetic data, get more out of lower-quality data, but each of those has diminishing returns relative to just having more good text. So the marginal pretraining dollar is buying you a bit less than it used to.

And then the third thing — and this is maybe the most important for understanding what's actually happening at the labs — is that pretraining isn't where the marginal gains are coming from anymore, so labs have shifted investment. Over the last couple of years, a huge fraction of the capability gains have come from post-training: reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, scaling up inference-time compute, reasoning models, agentic training. If you're a lab and you look at where a marginal dollar of compute gets you the most capability, RL has looked a lot more attractive than another 2x on pretraining. So in some sense pretraining looks like it's yielding slower progress partly because it's getting a smaller share of attention and compute.

I'd also add a more mundane point, which is that measured progress from pretraining was always a bit noisy and front-loaded. Going from GPT-3 to GPT-4 was a really visible jump. Subsequent scale-ups at the pretraining level have felt less dramatic in part because the benchmarks saturated and the things people care about — like whether the model can actually do a multi-hour software task — depend a lot on the post-training stack.

So I don't think the right takeaway is "scaling is dead." I think it's more like: the specific lever of pure pretraining scale is giving less per unit of effort than it did, the inputs to it are getting harder to scale, and there's another lever — RL and inference scaling — that's currently delivering more. The interesting question is how long that second lever keeps paying out, and whether we eventually have to return to scaling pretraining hard once RL starts to show its own diminishing returns. My guess is that overall capability progress continues at a pretty fast clip for at least the next few years, but the composition of where it comes from has changed, and I think people should update their models of AI progress accordingly rather than just reading off pretraining compute trends.

r001.rationale: The response says high-quality text is finite and that each way of expanding usable data has diminishing returns, so additional training data yields less marginal benefit.

r002.rationale: It calls the GPT-3 to GPT-4 jump visible but does not connect that improvement to larger datasets or more high-quality training tokens.

r003.rationale: It describes finite high-quality text and a gradual data headwind, but does not say current filtering has already captured much of the best available data.

r004.rationale: It says pure pretraining scale gives less per unit of effort, while explicitly rejecting the conclusion that scaling is dead.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between pretraining yielding smaller improvements and those improvements being less useful. You could keep getting fairly predictable reductions in prediction error without getting the same gains on the tasks you actually care about.

One possible explanation is that we’re running out of the most useful data. Early on, you can scale up both the model and the amount of high-quality text it sees. Eventually, adding more data means using material that’s more repetitive or less relevant, or showing the model the same material again. That could make additional compute less productive.

Another possibility is that some capabilities require a lot more compute than we initially expected. The jump from a model that can sometimes solve a problem to one that reliably solves it might be very expensive under the pretraining objective alone.

But I’d be cautious about concluding that we’ve established a slowdown in pretraining itself. What we observe is the performance of released systems, which mixes together pretraining, post-training, and how much computation they use when answering. It’s hard to separate those effects from the outside.

r001.rationale: It says that as added data becomes less relevant or repetitive, additional compute may become less productive, identifying lower marginal value from more training data as a possible cause.

r002.rationale: It does not mention GPT-3, GPT-4, or suggest that their improvement partly came from adding more high-quality training tokens.

r003.rationale: It says useful data may be running out, but does not say current filtering already captures much of the best available data.

r004.rationale: It allows that prediction error may keep falling predictably while the improvements become smaller or less useful, so pretraining gains need not disappear entirely.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between pretraining getting less effective and improvements in pretraining being less visible in the things we measure. Those can look pretty similar from the outside.

One possibility is that we’re running into limitations in the data. If you increase compute, you also want more useful training data, and it’s harder to keep increasing the amount of high-quality text. You can reuse data or add lower-quality data, but you might get less benefit from each additional unit of compute.

Another possibility is that the underlying improvements are continuing, but translating those improvements into capabilities people care about is getting harder. A model can get better at predicting text without becoming dramatically more reliable at doing a long, complicated task. And some benchmarks are becoming saturated, which makes progress harder to interpret.

I’m pretty uncertain about how much each of these explains. In particular, slower progress in pretraining wouldn’t necessarily imply slower progress in AI overall. You could still get substantial gains from post-training, from letting models spend more computation on a problem, or from better ways of using them.

r001.rationale: It says high-quality text is harder to expand and that additional compute may bring less benefit, identifying diminishing returns from scaling as a possible cause.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss GPT-3 to GPT-4 or attribute any part of their improvement to using more high-quality training tokens.

r003.rationale: It notes that high-quality text is harder to expand, but does not say current filtering already captures much of the best available data.

r004.rationale: It mentions possible diminishing benefits, but does not clearly state that pretraining gains continue rather than disappearing entirely.
